headline: Apartment Condominiums Drive Calgary's Price Declines as Summer Activity Slows
summary: Calgary sales eased to 1,904 units in July 2026, down 9.2% from last July and 13.3% from June, while new listings fell much harder at 15% to 3,323. Because listings pulled back faster than sales, the sales-to-new-listings ratio actually rose to 57% and inventory finished 4.2% below last July at 6,626 units, holding months of supply to a balanced 3.48. The total residential benchmark price slipped to $569,200, 2.0% below last July, but the decline is concentrated at the high-density end: apartment condominiums are down 8.4% and row homes 6.1%, while detached eased just 1.9% and semi-detached is essentially flat at 0.3% lower. CREB points to more than 17,000 apartment-style units still under construction as the pressure behind that split.
insights: The headline story in July was supply discipline, not weak demand. New listings fell 15% year-over-year to 3,323, a steeper drop than the 9.2% decline in sales, which pushed the sales-to-new-listings ratio up to 57% and left inventory at 6,626 units, 4.2% below last July. Months of supply sat at 3.48, comfortably balanced. Sellers who stayed on the sidelines are the reason prices held as well as they did.

Apartment condominiums account for most of the citywide price decline. The benchmark fell to $297,600, down 8.4% year-over-year, with 408 sales (off 20%) against 1,999 units of inventory and 4.90 months of supply. CREB's Ann-Marie Lurie tied the pressure directly to construction: more than 17,000 apartment-style units are still being built, and several consecutive years of high completions combined with a sharp drop in international migration have shifted conditions for higher-density housing since the second half of last year.

Row homes are the other soft spot, with the benchmark down 6.1% to $418,500 and 3.90 months of supply, the loosest of the ground-oriented types. Sales fell 23% and new listings fell 25%, so the segment is quiet on both sides rather than flooded. The steeper adjustment here reflects the same high-density pressure weighing on apartments, plus competition from new-home product.

Detached and semi-detached held the line. Detached sales of 1,012 were down just 2% with the benchmark easing 1.9% to $743,900 on a tight 2.90 months of supply, while semi-detached was the strongest segment in the city: sales up 6% year-over-year, a 62% sales-to-new-listings ratio, 2.89 months of supply, and a benchmark of $691,000 that is essentially flat at 0.3% below last July.

Where you looked mattered more than what you bought. The West district was the only part of Calgary with a rising benchmark in July at $723,200, up 0.9%, and the City Centre was close to flat at $576,200, down 0.7%. At the other end, the North East fell 6.6% to $466,400, the North 4.7% to $527,900, and the East 4.4% to $398,800. That is a seven-point spread between the strongest and weakest districts in a single city.

Around the region, Okotoks stayed the tightest market at 2.01 months of supply with its benchmark barely moved from June at $617,900. Cochrane loosened past four months of supply for the first time in the cycle at 4.22, with the benchmark easing to $575,800. Airdrie fell to $513,300, down 3.9% year-over-year and the softest of the four on an annual basis, while Chestermere held flat against June at $706,000 but carried 6.77 months of supply, the clearest oversupply anywhere in the region.
